newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa short-term money rates fall to 11-mth low.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa short-term money rates fall to 11-mth low.

text.p: Short-term rates fell to their lowest level in nearly a year on Thursday, helped by improved money market liquidity and speculation about a cut in official interest rates within the next few months, dealers said.
Deposit rates in the three-month area have moved to between 16.10 and 16.15 percent offered -- a 25 basis point fall so far this week -- to their lowest levels since July 11 last year.

Market talk of an interest rate cut has grown after the recent release of economic data supporting such a move, although economists believe a rate cut is unlikely until one to two months after July 1, when exchange controls on individuals will be relaxed.
Liquidity has also improved, with the shortage falling to 5.821 billion rand on Wednesday from 6.178 billion previously.

Roelf du Plooy, assistant general manager at the Reserve Bank's money and capital markets division, said that while the Reserve Bank was not uncomfortable with the current level of the shortage, it could drain liquidity from the market if it showed signs of improving further.
"If it looks like the shortage is going to drop substantially then we will have to do something again, maybe through swaps or selling other paper into the market.
"At this stage it could give the wrong signals to the market that the Bank is softening on its monetary policy," Du Plooy added.

But dealers said speculation about a cut in interest rates had spurred demand for NCDs (negotiable certificates of deposit) across the short-end of the curve. Twelve-month rates were last at 16.00 percent offered.

"There is buying right along the yield curve, purely on speculation about rate cuts," Jimmy Forbes, general manager at Nedcor Treasury, said. "Economists are looking at about three rate cuts by June next year so there is value in the market at the moment."
Traders said sentiment in the market had been buoyed this week by Monday night's official reserves data, which showed a 7.4 billion rand rise to a record 21.8 billion rand in May.
"With the reserves figures there has been quite a sentiment change," a senior trader said, adding investors were snapping up paper in anticipation of an interest rate cut.
Traders said they were surprised that the shortage had fallen as far as it had, and said it appeared that the central bank was battling to control the shortage.

Du Plooy said the shortage had fallen on Wednesday as a result of a mismatch in government flows, and had been helped lower in recent weeks by foreign inflows and the unwinding of swaps used to mop up liquidity from the proceeds of the partial privatisation of telecommunications utility Telkom.
"We have seen a lot of foreign inflows into the country and that has definitely added some liquidity to the money market."
He also said that the unwinding of the swaps, which was timed to coincide with normal month-end outflows such as public and private sector salaries, had also expanded liquidity.
Bank rate, currently 17 percent, was last hiked by one percentage point in November last year.
